prompt: After remote loaded the shop, which client address did app's log show?
hint: Who opened the connection to app?

choices.why: That is in www's log; app never saw remote.

choices.text: 192.0.2.80, the proxy's
choices.why: Right. The proxy made its own request.

choices.text: 203.0.113.2, the firewall's outside address
choices.why: fw routes; it does not rewrite addresses here.

choices.text: No address; HTTP carries none
choices.why: The log line starts with the client's address.

prompt: Why may app trust X-Forwarded-For in this lab, when an application reachable from the internet should not?
hint: Who is able to write that header on a request that reaches app?

choices.text: The header is signed by nginx
choices.why: It is plain text; nothing signs it.

choices.text: HTTPS protects every header from being changed
choices.why: TLS protects in transit; the client writes what it likes.

choices.text: The firewall lets only www reach app, and www writes the header itself
choices.why: Right. Directly reachable, a client could send any value.

choices.text: X-Forwarded-For carries the address from the IP header
choices.why: It is an HTTP header anyone may send.

prompt: What does it mean that the proxy terminates TLS?
hint: Where does the encrypted connection end?

choices.text: The encryption ends on www, which holds the key
choices.why: Right, and the next hop is a new connection.

choices.text: It passes the encrypted bytes through to app unchanged
choices.why: That would be a TCP pass-through, not termination.

choices.text: It refuses clients that offer TLS 1.1
choices.why: That is ssl_protocols, a separate setting.

choices.text: It closes TLS sessions after one request
choices.why: Terminate here means where the encryption ends.

prompt: What does putting a reverse proxy in front of the application give? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

choices.text: One place that holds the certificate
choices.why: TLS ends there.

choices.text: A place to refuse requests before the application sees them
choices.why: The rest of the lesson uses it.

choices.text: The application's machine stays unreachable from the internet
choices.why: remote's direct attempt timed out.

choices.text: The application's own bugs stop mattering
choices.why: A proxy passes valid-looking requests through, bugs and all.

prompt: Match each request from remote to the answer the proxy gave.
hint: The captures in the section.

prompt: Why does the lesson turn server_tokens off?
hint: Is it a defence, and what does it stop volunteering?

choices.text: It patches known vulnerabilities in nginx
choices.why: It only changes a header.

choices.text: It makes the server invisible to scanners
choices.why: It still answers, and says nginx.

choices.text: A version tells a stranger what to try first
choices.why: Right. Not a defence, just nothing volunteered.

choices.text: HTTP/2 requires the header to be empty
choices.why: No such requirement.

prompt: Every refusal in this section was written without knowing what an attack looks like. What were they written from instead?
hint: Compare with the firewall's policy drop.

choices.text: A list of attack signatures kept by the vendor
choices.why: That is the WAF's approach, the next sections.

choices.text: The access log of past incidents
choices.why: Nothing here came from past incidents.

choices.text: What the shop legitimately receives
choices.why: Right. Allow what is used, refuse the rest.

choices.text: The defaults of the OWASP Core Rule Set, as shipped
choices.why: CRS is not loaded yet in this section.

prompt: The nginx directive that refuses a request body above a size is client_max_body___.
hint: Read the example's fourth part.

prompt: Of remote's 30 quick requests, how many were refused with 429?
hint: uniq -c counted them.

prompt: Straight after remote's burst, laptop's request was served. Why?
hint: What is the limit keyed on?

choices.text: The LAN is exempt from rate limits by default
choices.why: Nothing exempts it; it has its own counter.

choices.text: It has a counter of its own
choices.why: Right: $binary_remote_addr, one counter per address.

choices.text: The burst had already refilled completely
choices.why: remote was still over its limit.

choices.text: laptop used HTTPS and remote used HTTP
choices.why: Both used HTTPS.

prompt: Why set limit_req_status 429 instead of keeping nginx's default?
hint: What does the default say to the client?

choices.text: 429 makes the limit stricter
choices.why: The status code does not change the rate.

choices.text: The default closes the connection and sends nothing back to the client
choices.why: The default answers 503.

choices.text: Browsers retry a 503 forever
choices.why: That is not why.

choices.text: 503 claims the server is broken; 429 says too many requests
choices.why: Right. The status should say what happened.

prompt: Where does a per-address rate limit get the wrong answer? Choose all that apply.
hint: One address is assumed to be one client.

choices.text: A whole office behind one NAT address
choices.why: They share one counter and hit it together.

choices.text: Traffic spread over thousands of addresses
choices.why: Each stays under the limit.

choices.text: One script hammering from one address
choices.why: That is exactly the case it handles.

choices.text: A client asking once a minute
choices.why: Nowhere near the limit, correctly served.

prompt: In detection-only mode, the test string returned 200. What did the WAF do?
hint: Look at the audit log.

choices.text: Nothing; the rules were not loaded
choices.why: 921 rules loaded.

choices.text: Scored it and logged that it would have blocked
choices.why: Right: three matches, score 15, rule 949110.

choices.text: Removed the script tag and passed the rest
choices.why: ModSecurity here does not rewrite requests.

choices.text: Blocked it, but the proxy's cache answered
choices.why: There is no cache in this configuration.

prompt: What total anomaly score did the test string reach?
hint: Rule 949110's message.

prompt: With CRS's default threshold of 5, what is the smallest set of matches that blocks a request?
hint: A critical match is worth 5.

choices.text: Three matches of any severity
choices.why: Points add up by severity, not by count.

choices.text: One critical match
choices.why: Right. The false positive in the next section scored exactly 5.

choices.text: Every rule of one category matching
choices.why: Far more than needed.

choices.text: Any match at paranoia level 2 or above
choices.why: Paranoia decides which rules run, not the threshold.

prompt: A customer reads another customer's order by changing the number in /orders/17 to /orders/18. Why does the WAF not stop it?
hint: What does a WAF know about?

choices.text: The request was encrypted
choices.why: TLS ended at the proxy, where the WAF reads.

choices.text: The paranoia level was too low
choices.why: No level sees ownership of an order.

choices.text: The WAF inspects POST bodies and lets GET requests through uninspected
choices.why: The test string was a GET.

choices.text: It knows attack patterns, not who owns what
choices.why: Right. It is a flaw in the application's logic.

prompt: The support message containing SQL was refused. What kind of result is that?
hint: Was the request legitimate? Was the WAF right about what it saw?

choices.text: A false positive
choices.why: Right: legitimate, and the rule saw SQL correctly.

choices.text: A false negative
choices.why: That would be an attack let through.

choices.text: A true positive
choices.why: The request was not an attack.

choices.text: A parsing error in the WAF
choices.why: Rule 942100 matched as designed.

prompt: Order these fixes for the false positive from broadest to narrowest.
hint: The narrowest is the one the lesson used.
items: switch the whole WAF to detection-only
remove rule 942100 from the whole site
trap: Each step keeps more of the protection running; the last keeps everything except one field for one rule.

prompt: After the exclusion, which of these requests to /support are still refused? Choose all that apply.
hint: The exclusion names one rule and one field.

choices.text: comment=<script>alert(1)</script>
choices.why: The XSS rules were never touched.

choices.text: name=select id from orders where total > 100
choices.why: Only comment was excluded.

choices.text: comment=select id from orders where total > 100
choices.why: That is what the exclusion lets through.

choices.text: comment=my order has not arrived
choices.why: Nothing in it matches any rule.

prompt: The shop adds a page for customers to upload photos of damaged goods, and uploads fail with 413. What is the right change?
hint: Narrow, like the exclusion.

choices.text: Raise client_max_body_size for the whole site
choices.why: Every form would then accept large bodies.

choices.text: Switch the WAF to detection-only
choices.why: 413 comes from nginx's size limit, not the WAF.

choices.text: A larger limit on the upload page alone
choices.why: Right, as the example's note said.

choices.text: Remove the limit and rely on the rate limit
choices.why: A rate limit counts requests, not their size.

prompt: Match each problem to the control in this lesson that handles it.
hint: Four controls, four problems.

pairs.left: a script requesting the login page 200 times a second
a request carrying script tags in a parameter
a DELETE request the shop never uses
the admin pages seen from the internet

prompt: A request arrives at www. Which check happens last?
hint: app is the last hop.

choices.text: fw accepting TCP to port 443
choices.why: That is before www sees anything.

choices.text: TLS being terminated
choices.why: It must happen before the request can be read.

choices.text: The WAF scoring the request
choices.why: It happens before the proxy passes it on.

choices.text: app handling it
choices.why: Right. It only arrives if every check before it passed.
